politica.por_que: Las 30 consultas de evaluación se trazan **completas** (`el registro de decisiones la política de trazado`). No son dato de un tercero: son obras de nuestro propio held-out, versionadas con el ground truth porque son el **instrumento de medición** (el registro de decisiones). Trazarlas enteras cumple las técnicas avanzadas aisladas por medición, la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura y el criterio de costo sin tocar el compromiso de privacidad.

aic:109819.texto: Piet Mondrian, a painter of the revolutionary international movement De Stijl (the Style), argued that "the straight line tells the truth." Why, then, we might wonder, would he choose to hang a painting off axis, where its edges imply dynamic diagonals? Among other motivations, rotating the canvas allowed Mondrian to reconsider a question he spent his career exploring, namely, the relationship between the contents of a painting and what contains them. In Lozenge Composition, the squared-off black lines imply enclosure, while a single line (above the blue area) extends to the slanted edge, suggesting extension beyond the canvas. This implication of what might lie beyond also prompted Mondrian to invoke the full expanse of the wall by hanging diagonal paintings well above eye level.
aic:109819.title: Lozenge Composition with Yellow, Black, Blue, Red, and Gray

aic:56905.texto: In the early 1870s James McNeill Whistler took a radical step toward abstraction with his Nocturnes series. In keeping with his art-for-art’s-sake creed, these works capture the stillness of evening while evoking a connection to music. Unlike his earlier marine paintings, the subject of this work—an inlet along the English Channel near Southampton—is obscured by the approaching night. Large shipping vessels appear as ghostly shapes, reduced to shadowy forms by the deepening twilight, while the only points of brightness come from the subtle reflections of lights and the fragmented orb of the moon. The setting thus serves primarily as a vehicle for Whistler’s interest in the harmonies of muted color amid darkness.
aic:56905.title: Nocturne: Blue and Gold—Southampton Water

cma:143278.texto: During the 1910s, Piet Mondrian’s art progressed from Cubism to an increasingly abstract style based on the form of a grid. He completely abandoned the representation of natural appearances, limiting himself to horizontal and vertical rectangles and three primary colors (red, yellow, and blue) along with black and white. Intensely intellectual and deeply philosophical, Mondrian believed that following the devastation of World War I, such abstract compositions could contribute to a more harmonious society by communicating in a universal, visual language.

cma:715339.texto: The Spanish artist María Blanchard worked in Paris as a Cubist between 1916 and 1919. In Still Life, she portrayed multiple, simultaneous viewpoints in an abstract style based on geometry and flat planes. Although other Cubists used collage elements in their work, Blanchard was unique in her use of three-dimensional elements to create an image that fluctuates between the concrete and the illusionary. During her lifetime, Blanchard was celebrated by her fellow Cubists, and she shared studios with Juan Gris and Diego Riviera, the latter of whom described her as producing Cubism’s “finest works, apart from our master, Picasso.”

cma:84662.texto: As reflected in the two-dimensionality and color blocking in this painting, Denis believed a painting was "a flat surface covered with colors assembled in a certain order."

cma:84662.texto: A devout Catholic, Maurice Denis sought to create what he described as “imperishable icons.” In this small painting, he used flat planes of intense colors to conjure emotion in the viewer. Here, a somber group of women, depicted as amorphous black forms, gather around an orange figure of Christ on the cross. The sky is a reddish-purple streaked with green clouds. Pink angels flank the crucified Christ whose head is haloed in brilliant yellow. In this painting, the daring young artist combined religious fervor with unprecedented visual experimentation.
cma:84662.title: The Orange Christ

salida.nota_de_idioma: el contrato de la salida citada / el criterio de idioma: la explicación en **español**, el fragmento citado **textual en inglés, sin traducir**.    Presenta una atmósfera de colores apagados y armonías de tonos suaves, con una composición que evoca la abstracción y la música. [1]
   La composición no es geométrica ni estrictamente ordenada, sino que representa un paisaje nocturno con formas difusas y sombras.
   No es una composición geométrica al óleo del siglo XX.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “In the early 1870s James McNeill Whistler took a radical step toward abstraction with his Nocturnes series. In keeping with his art-for-art’s-sake creed, these works capture the stillness of evening while evoking a connection to music. Unlike his earlier marine paintings, the subject of this work—an inlet along the English Channel near Southampton—is obscured by the approaching night. Large shipping vessels appear as ghostly shapes, reduced to shadowy forms by the deepening twilight, while the only points of brightness come from the subtle reflections of lights and the fragmented orb of the moon. The setting thus serves primarily as a vehicle for Whistler’s interest in the harmonies of muted color amid darkness.”
       https://www.artic.edu/artworks/56905 · CC BY 4.0
       “Nocturne: Blue and Gold—Southampton Water”, James McNeill Whistler. Art Institute of Chicago. Texto bajo CC BY 4.0 — https://www.artic.edu/artworks/56905

5. **Still Life**
   María Blanchard · c. 1916 · oil, sand, and mixed media collage on canvas
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/2026.37

   La obra es al óleo con arena y collage sobre lienzo, realizada alrededor de 1916, en el siglo XX. [1]
   Es una composición abstracta basada en la geometría y planos planos, con múltiples puntos de vista simultáneos. [1]
   La obra combina elementos bidimensionales y tridimensionales, lo que genera una imagen fluctuante entre lo concreto y lo ilusorio. [2]
   Los colores no son particularmente suaves, sino que se perciben planos y contrastantes, y la composición es ordenada en términos geométricos.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “The Spanish artist María Blanchard worked in Paris as a Cubist between 1916 and 1919. In Still Life, she portrayed multiple, simultaneous viewpoints in an abstract style based on geometry and flat planes. Although other Cubists used collage elements in their work, Blanchard was unique in her use of three-dimensional elements to create an image that fluctuates between the concrete and the illusionary. During her lifetime, Blanchard was celebrated by her fellow Cubists, and she shared studios with Juan Gris and Diego Riviera, the latter of whom described her as producing Cubism’s “finest works, apart from our master, Picasso.””
       https://clevelandart.org/art/2026.37 · CC0 1.0
   [2] “This work of art, which combines two- and three-dimensional elements, challenges the long-established notion that an artwork should consist of a single medium.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/2026.37 · CC0 1.0

La identidad fija **las entradas, no la salida** —una salida no determinista con la misma entrada es el dato que el muestreo fijado, registrado y con su variabilidad medida mide—, así que lleva **ordinal** y la regla de que un id determina su contenido no aplica.
